title: K pairs with the smallest sums → the k-th smallest sum
label: single
statement: Two arrays `a` and `b` are sorted in ascending order. Return the **k pairs** `(a[i], b[j])` with the **smallest sums**, smallest first (ties: smaller i, then smaller j). If there are fewer than k pairs, return them all.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Two arrays `a` and `b` are sorted in ascending order. Return the **k pairs** `(a[i], b[j])` with the **smallest sums**, smallest first (ties: smaller i, then smaller j). If there are fewer than k pairs, return them all.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Are both arrays sorted? (Yes — that is what makes the heap work.)
- Tie order? (By i, then j — so it can be tested.)
- Can values be negative or large? (Yes — sum in long.)
- k larger than |a|·|b|? (Return every pair.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Think of the sums as a grid: row i, column j. Each row is sorted. So the next smallest pair is always at the front of some row — keep one "next" pair per row in a min-heap.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: I would say, before coding: "A." min-heap with one frontier pair per row (i, next j); pop the smallest, push the next pair in that row — O(k log min(k, |a|)) and never all |a|·|b| pairs."

learn.title: 8 · Complexity

**Level 2 — Complexity**

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases

- *Overflow?* — Two ints can sum past int.MaxValue — use long.

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Generating all |a|·|b| pairs and sorting — huge for big arrays.
- Pushing both (i+1, j) and (i, j+1) without a visited set → duplicates.
- int overflow in the sum.
- Seeding the heap with all rows when k is small.
